entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen9406" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Seeming Prosperity of the Wicked, and the Real Prosperity of the Godly</title> <div sID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> The bond of connection between <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1-Ps.36.12">Psa 36:1-12</reference> and 37 is their similarity of contents, which here and there extends even to accords of expression. The fundamental thought running through the whole Psalm is at once expressed in the opening verses: Do not let the prosperity of the ungodly be a source of vexation to thee, but wait on the Lord; for the prosperity of the ungodly will suddenly come to an end, and the issue determines between the righteous and the unrighteous. Hence Tertullian calls this Psalm <hi type="italic">providentiae speculum</hi>; Isodore, <hi type="italic">potio contra murmur</hi>; and Luther, <hi type="italic">vestis piorum, cui adscriptum: Hic Sanctorum patientia est</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.12">Rev 14:12</reference>). This fundamental thought the poet does not expand in strophes of ordinary compass, but in shorter utterances of the proverbial form following the order of the letters of the alphabet, and not without some repetitions and recurrences to a previous thought, in order to impress it still more convincingly and deeply upon the mind. The Psalm belongs therefore to the series Ps 9 and <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference>, - all alphabetical Psalms of David, of whose language, cheering, high-flown, thoughtful, and at the same time so easy and unartificial, and withal elegant, this Psalm is fully worthy. The structure of the proverbial utterances is almost entirely tetrastichic; though ד, כ, and ק are tristichs, and ח (which is twice represented, though perhaps unintentionally), נ, and ת are pentastichs. The ע is apparently wanting; but, on closer inspection, the originally separated strophes ס and ע are only run into one another by the division of the verses. The ע strophe begins with לעולם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">Psa 37:28</reference></hi>, and forms a tetrastich, just like the ס. The fact that the preposition ל stands before the letter next in order need not confuse one. The ת, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39">Psa 37:39</reference>, also begins with ותשׁועת. The homogeneous beginnings, זמם רשׁע, לוה רשׁע, צופה רשׁע, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12">Psa 37:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">Psa 37:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">Psa 37:32</reference>, seem, as Hitzig remarks, to be designed to give prominence to the pauses in the succession of the proverbial utterances.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2">Psa 37:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> Olshausen observes, “The poet keeps entirely to the standpoint of the old Hebrew doctrine of recompense, which the Book of Job so powerfully refutes.” But, viewed in the light of the final issue, all God’s government is really in a word righteous recompense; and the Old Testament theodicy is only inadequate in so far as the future, which adjusts all present inconsistencies, is still veiled. Meanwhile the punitive justice of God does make itself manifest, as a rule, in the case of the ungodly even in the present world; even their dying is usually a fearful end to their life’s prosperity. This it is which the poet means here, and which is also expressed by Job himself in the Book of Job, Job 27:1. With התחרה, to grow hot or angry (distinct from תּחרה, to emulate, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>), alternates קנּא, to get into a glow, <hi type="italic">excandescentia</hi>, whether it be the restrained heat of sullen envy, or the incontrollable heat of impetuous zeal which would gladly call down fire from heaven. This first distich has been transferred to the Book of Proverbs, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.19">Pro 24:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">Pro 23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.1">Pro 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31">Pro 3:31</reference>; and in general we may remark that this Psalm is one of the Davidic patterns for the Salomonic gnome system. The form ימּלוּ is, according to Gesenius, Olshausen, and Hitzig, <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of מלל, cognate אמל, they wither away, pausal form for ימּלוּ like יתּממוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.28">Psa 102:28</reference>; but the signification to cut off also is secured to the verb מלל by the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נמל, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.11">Gen 17:11</reference>, whence <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ימּלוּ = ימּלּוּ; vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>; Job 18:16. ירק דּשׁא is a genitival combination: the green (<hi type="italic">viror</hi>) of young vigorous vegetation.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3-Ps.37.4">Psa 37:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9409" type="x-p"/> The “land” is throughout this Psalm the promised possession (<hi type="italic">Heilsgut</hi>), viz., the land of Jahve’s presence, which has not merely a glorious past, but also a future rich in promises; and will finally, ore perfectly than under Joshua, become the inheritance of the true Israel. It is therefore to be explained: enjoy the quiet sure habitation which God gives thee, and diligently cultivate the virtue of faithfulness. The two imperatives in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Psa 37:3</reference></hi>, since there are two of them (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">Psa 37:27</reference>) and the first is without any conjunctive <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, have the appearance of being continued admonitions, not promises; and consequently אמוּנה is not an adverbial accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.75">Psa 119:75</reference> (Ewald), but the object to רעה, to pasture, to pursue, to practise (Syriac רדף, Hos 12:2); cf. רעה, רע, one who interests himself in any one, or anything; Beduin <hi type="italic">râ‛â = ṣâḥb</hi>, of every kind of closer relationship (<hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenländ. Zeitschr.</hi> v. 9). In <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>, ויתן is an apodosis: delight in Jahve (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.22.26">Job 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>), so will He grant thee the desire (משׁאלת, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.5">Psa 20:5</reference>) of thy heart; for he who, entirely severed from the creature, finds his highest delight in God, cannot desire anything that is at enmity with God, but he also can desire nothing that God, with whose will his own is thoroughly blended in love, would refuse him.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference> <div eID="gen9410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> The verb דּמם, with its derivatives (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.2">Psa 62:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.6">Psa 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28">Lam 3:28</reference>), denotes resignation, i.e., a quiet of mind which rests on God, renounces all self-help, and submits to the will of God. התחולל (from הוּל, to be in a state of tension, to wait) of the inward gathering of one’s self together in hope intently directed towards God, as in <hi type="italic">B. Berachoth 30b</hi> is a synonym of התחונן, and as it were reflexive of חלּה of the collecting one’s self to importunate prayer. With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference></hi> the primary tone of the whole Psalm is struck anew. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference></hi> compare the definition of the mischief-maker in Pro 24:8.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.8-Ps.37.9">Psa 37:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9412" type="x-p"/> On הרף (let alone), <hi type="italic">imper. apoc. Hiph</hi>., instead of הרפּה, vid., Ges. §75, rem. 15. אך להרע is a clause to itself (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>): it tends only to evil-doing, it ends only in thy involving thyself in sin. The final issue, without any need that thou shouldst turn sullen, is that the מרעים, like to whom thou dost make thyself by such passionate murmuring and displeasure, will be cut off, and they who, turning from the troublous present, make Jahve the ground and aim of their hope, shall inherit the land (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">Psa 25:13</reference>). It is the end, the final and consequently eternal end, that decides the matter.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference> <div eID="gen9417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9418" type="x-p"/> With כּי the preceding assertion is confirmed by its opposite (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>). כּיקר בּרים forms a fine play in sound; יקר is a substantivized adjective like גּדל ekil evitcejda, Exo 15:16. Instead of בעשׁן, it is not to be read כּעשׁן, Hos 13:3; the ב is secured by <reference osisRef="Ps.102.4">Psa 102:4</reference>; Psa 78:33. The idea is, that they vanish into smoke, i.e., are resolved into it, or also, that they vanish in the manner of smoke, which is first thick, but then becomes thinner and thinner till it disappears (Rosenmüller, Hupfeld, Hitzig); both expressions are admissible as to fact and as to the language, and the latter is commended by בּהבל, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.33">Psa 78:33</reference>, cf. בּצלם, Psa 39:7. בעשׁן belongs to the first, regularly accented כּלוּ; for the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> by בעשׂן is the substitute for <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, which never can be used where at least two syllables do not precede the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi> tone (vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 503). The second כּלוּ has the accent on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. for a change (Ew. §194, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), i.e., variation of the rhythm (cf. למה   למה, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Psa 42:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>; עורי   עורי, Jdg 5:12, and on <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>), and in particular here on account of its pausal position (cf. ערוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>).

The confirmation of <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference> is not inappropriate (as Hitzig considers it, who places <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference> after <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>): in that ever deeper downfall of the ungodly, and in that charitableness of the righteous, which becomes more and more easy to him by reason of his prosperity, the curse and blessing of God, which shall be revealed in the end of the earthly lot of both the righteous and the ungodly, are even now foretold. Whilst those who reject the blessing of God are cut off, the promise given to the patriarchs is fulfilled in the experience of those who are blessed of God, in all its fulness.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.23-Ps.37.24">Psa 37:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen9419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9420" type="x-p"/> By Jahve (מן, ἀπό, almost equivalent to ὑπό with the passive, as in <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Ecc 12:11</reference>, and in a few other passages) are a man’s steps made firm, established; not: ordered or directed (lxx, Jerome, κατευθύνεται), which, according to the extant usage of the language, would be הוּכנוּ (passive of הכין, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Pro 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">Jer 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.6">2Ch 27:6</reference>), whereas כּוננוּ, the <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> of כּונן, is to be understood according to Psa 40:3. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25-Ps.37.26">Psa 37:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen9420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9421" type="x-p"/> There is an old theological rule: <hi type="italic">promissiones corporales intelligendae sunt cum exceptione crucis et castigationis</hi>. Temporary forsakenness and destitution the Psalm does not deny: it is indeed even intended to meet the conflict of doubt which springs up in the minds of the God-fearing out of certain conditions and circumstances that are seemingly contradictory to the justice of God; and this it does, by contrasting that which in the end abides with that which is transitory, and in fact without the knowledge of any final decisive adjustment in a future world; and it only solves its problem, in so far as it is placed in the light of the New Testament, which already dawns in the Book of Ecclesiastes.

The imperative שׁכן, which is there hortatory, is found here with the ו of sequence in the sense of a promise: and continue, doing such things, to dwell for ever = so shalt thou, etc. (שׁכן, pregnant as in Ps 102:29, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>). Nevertheless the imperative retains its meaning even in such instances, inasmuch as the exhortation is given to share in the reward of duty at the same time with the discharge of it. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35-Ps.37.36">Psa 37:35-36</reference> עריץ (after the form צדּיק) is coupled with רשׁע, must as these two words alternate in <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">Job 15:20</reference> : a terror-inspiring, tyrannical evil-doer; cf. besides also Job 5:3. The participle in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Psa 37:35</reference></hi> forms a clause by itself: <hi type="italic">et se diffundens</hi>, scil. <hi type="italic">erat</hi>. The lxx and Jerome translate as though it were כארז הלבנן, “like the cedars of Lebanon,” instead of כאזרח רענן. But אזרח רענן is the expression for an oak, terebinth, or the like, that has brown from time immemorial in its native soil, and has in the course of centuries attained a gigantic size in the stem, and a wide-spreading overhanging head. ויּעבר does not mean: then he vanished away (Hupfeld and others); for עבר in this sense is not suitable to a tree. Luther correctly renders it: <hi type="italic">man ging vorüber</hi>, one (they) passed by, Ges. §137, 3. The lxx, Syriac, and others, by way of lightening the difficulty, render it: then I passed by.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37-Ps.37.38">Psa 37:37-38</reference> תּם might even be taken as neuter for תּם, and ישׂר for ישׁר; but in this case the poet would have written רעה instead of ראה; שׁמר is therefore used as, e.g., in 1Sa 1:12. By כּי that to which attention is specially called is introduced. The man of peace has a totally different lot from the evil-doer who delights in contention and persecution. As the fruit of his love of peace he has אחרית, a future, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">Pro 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.14">Pro 24:14</reference>, viz., in his posterity, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.20">Pro 24:20</reference>; whereas the apostates are altogether blotted out; not merely they themselves, but even the posterity of the ungodly is cut off, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Amo 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">Amo 9:1</reference>; Eze 23:25. To them remains no posterity to carry forward their name, their אחרית is devoted to destruction (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference> with Num 24:20).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39-Ps.37.40">Psa 37:39-40</reference> <div eID="gen9426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9427" type="x-p"/> The salvation of the righteous cometh from Jahve; it is therefore characterized, in accordance with its origin, as sure, perfect, and enduring for ever. מעוּזּם is an apposition; the <hi type="italic">plena scriptio</hi> serves, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.33">2Sa 22:33</reference>, to indicate to us that מעוז is meant in this passage to signify not a fortress, but a hiding-place, a place of protection, a refuge, in which sense Arab. <hi type="italic">ma'âd‛llh</hi> (the protection of God) and <hi type="italic">m‛âḏwjh‛llh</hi> (the protection of God’s presence) is an Arabic expression (also used as a formula of an oath); vid., moreover on Psa 31:3. The moods of sequence in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.40">Psa 37:40</reference> are <hi type="italic">aoristi gnomici</hi>. The parallelism in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.40">Psa 37:40</reference></hi> is progressive after the manner of the Psalms of degrees. The short confirmatory clause <hi type="italic">kichā'subo</hi> forms an expressive closing cadence.  <chapter eID="Ps.37"/> <div eID="gen9427" type="x-p"/>
